newsitem.title: CANADA: Imperial faces upstream, downstream hits.
newsitem.headline: Imperial faces upstream, downstream hits.

text.p: Imperial Oil Ltd, Canada's biggest energy company, faces operational and supply problems in both its upstream and downstream businesses as a result of Interprovincial Pipe Line Co's shutdown, an Imperial official said on Monday.
"It's certainly not good all around," Al Dedesko, Imperial's manager of crude oil supply, said in a phone interview. "And not just us -- the entire industry is being severely impacted."

A massive weekend outage on the Interprovincial system forced half of Canada's total oil supply to a halt and the pipeline company, owned by IPL Energy Inc, said it would be at least Wednesday until the situation was fixed.
"In our case, we're going to end up with heavy crude oil being shut in in western Canada and simultaneously we're going to start running short of crude oil for our Ontario refineries," Dedesko said.
"What we are doing, along with the rest of the industry, is trying to maximize crude oil for Ontario coming up through the U.S. systems."
He said many Chicago refiners impacted by the outage were employing the same strategy for trying to gain supply.
Imperial, 69.6 percent owned by Exxon Corp, operates refineries at Nanticoke and Sarnia, Ontario with combined capacity of 186,000 barrels per day.
Dedesko said he was unable to recall a pipeline outage as severe is the current one on IPL.
"Nothing at all like this. We have had interruptions on the Interprovincial system, but nothing of this magnitude where nothing at all is going to move for a four-day period," he said.
Imperial is also Canada's largest producer of crude oil, in the fourth quarter of 1996 pumping an average of 248,000 barrels per day.

Of the total, about 100,000 barrels per day flows from the company's massive Cold Lake heavy oil project in northern Alberta, where steam is pumped into the ground to allow the thick oil to be pumped to the surface.
Dedesko said Imperial would have to cut back production at Cold Lake after all storage options -- which include IPL's own facilities at Edmonton -- are exhausted.

"That definitely is problematic," he said. "We can shut in a fair bit of it and whatever would need to keep getting produced, we would look for outlets locally, for example our own refinery at Edmonton."
